title: Rocket Report: SpaceX completes launch triple-header; Rocket Lab nets big contract
gist: SpaceX's 14th Starship flight reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and SpaceX flew three launches in 13 hours. Rocket Lab signed a 20-launch Electron deal with Synspective, NASA is backing Starliner and Vulcan human-rating as Falcon 9/Dragon retirement nears, and Blue Origin seeks FAA approval for 50 New Glenn launches a year.

insights.claim: SpaceX's Starship reached low-Earth orbital velocity for the first time on its 14th test flight, after all prior flights were deliberately flown suborbital.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Orbital capability is the gate to Starship carrying real payloads, so watch for the cadence of operational Starship launches.
insights.locator: Starship reaches new heights in low-Earth orbit

insights.claim: Starship deployed the first 26 Starlink V3 satellites, which are too large for Falcon 9, which SpaceX is positioning as a major unlock for Starlink growth.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Starlink capacity growth now depends on Starship, which makes Starship reliability a driver of SpaceX's broadband economics.
insights.quote: unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink
insights.locator: What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight

insights.claim: The Starship flight was cut from a planned 10-hour test to three hours after a Raptor engine failed during ascent, yet the vehicle still made a pinpoint splashdown at a backup site north of Hawaii.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Engine-out tolerance and precision recovery are positive signs, but the shortened test means some orbital objectives were left untested.

insights.claim: SpaceX held Starship back from orbit on earlier flights over safety concerns about stranding the huge rocket in space, and only chose orbit after several successful suborbital flights in a row.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Incremental, risk-gated testing explains the 14-flight timeline, which is useful for forecasting future milestone pacing.
insights.locator: Welcome to Edition 9.13 of the Rocket Report

insights.claim: SpaceX flew two Falcon 9 launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in under 13 hours, making three launches and four booster landings in one day, one of its busiest days ever.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Demonstrated launch tempo reinforces SpaceX's cost and cadence lead over competitors.
insights.locator: SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours

insights.claim: Falcon Heavy launched a classified payload for the National Reconnaissance Office for the first time, into a highly inclined orbit from Florida.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Continued national-security heavy-lift work is a durable revenue stream for SpaceX.

insights.claim: The Transporter-18 rideshare carried 130 payloads to polar Sun-synchronous orbit, with customers including Google, Starfish Space, Planet Labs and ICEYE.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Satellite startups and remote-sensing firms depend on SpaceX rideshare, which is a concentration risk for the sector.

insights.claim: Falcon 9 rideshare launches will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX moves to the much larger Starship, which could disrupt the cheap, predictable access that many commercial satellite startups rely on.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Small-launch and rideshare alternatives such as Rocket Lab may benefit if Falcon rideshare ends.
insights.quote: These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years

insights.claim: Rocket Lab signed its largest Electron launch agreement to date, 20 missions for Japanese radar-satellite operator Synspective, lifting Synspective's total bookings to 47 launches, 13 of them already flown.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A multi-launch anchor customer adds backlog visibility for Rocket Lab's Electron line.
insights.locator: Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet

insights.claim: NASA will pay Boeing $359 million to rebuild Starliner's overheating reaction control thrusters, exercise options for two more Starliner flights (six total), and certify ULA's Vulcan for crewed missions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Boeing and ULA retain government-backed crew-launch roles, though Starliner execution risk remains.
insights.locator: NASA will pay to human-rate ULA's Vulcan rocket

insights.claim: NASA is preserving a second path to orbit for its astronauts because SpaceX is nearing retirement of Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon, after which Starliner would likely be the only commercial means of launching US crews.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Policy support for Starliner and Vulcan reflects concern about single-provider dependence on SpaceX.

insights.claim: Starliner flights beyond the six NASA has now ordered would need a new rocket such as Vulcan, because the Atlas V is no longer in production.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Vulcan human-rating is the critical dependency for Starliner's long-term viability.

insights.claim: Crew-13 launched on Falcon 9 and Dragon for a six-month ISS stay after a delay of several weeks to fix a leaky Dragon propulsion valve, which was cut out and replaced by welding in a new one.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A Dragon hardware issue caused a multi-week slip, though SpaceX's 21st crewed launch otherwise went smoothly.

insights.claim: Canada Rocket Company is skipping small launchers to build the R-2, a Falcon 9-like medium-lift rocket with 12.5 metric tons to LEO capacity, targeting a launch by 2032.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A 2032 target means any Canadian competitor is years away from the market.

insights.claim: Canada Rocket Company's CEO argues that a rocket development program cannot be de-risked by building a smaller rocket first, a view that favors going straight to medium or heavy lift.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: This challenges the usual small-launcher-first path and suggests new entrants may skip Electron-class vehicles.
insights.quote: you're not going to be able to de-risk a rocket development program by building a smaller rocket

insights.claim: US trade threats and tariffs toward Canada have crystallized Canadian interest in sovereign space access, and the Canadian government made first awards this spring to NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics and Canada Rocket Company.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Geopolitical friction is pushing allies to fund domestic launch capacity, a possible tailwind for non-US launch suppliers.

insights.claim: Portuguese firm Omnidea bought the assets and IP of collapsed Scottish rocket maker Orbex to set up UK operations, while Orbex's Prime rocket, which never neared a launch pad, appears to be dead.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: European small-launch consolidation continues, with component suppliers absorbing failed launch developers.
insights.locator: Portuguese company acquires what's left of Orbex

insights.claim: Blue Origin is asking the FAA to raise New Glenn launches from Cape Canaveral's Launch Complex 36 from 12 to 50 per year, with 50 drone-ship booster landings and up to 100 static-fire tests, while still recovering from a May pad explosion.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The filing shows ambition to compete with SpaceX on cadence, but it is a draft environmental assessment, not demonstrated capability.
insights.locator: Blue Origin foresees growing launch cadence

insights.claim: Blue Origin has not attempted payload fairing recovery on any of New Glenn's three launches so far, though the proposal covers it.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Full reuse economics for New Glenn are still unproven.
